paragraphs: The Fei River was narrow. Only after three straight days of autumn rain had flooded the sandbars did it seem at all broad. It wound southward past Shouchun, where the wind whitened the reed flowers and the muddy shores held the delicate clawprints of waterbirds. Without this war it would have been merely a river on which the people of Huainan ferried passengers, caught fish, and watered their fields.

By the time the Qin vanguard arrived, not even the first pontoon bridge had been built, yet grain wagons already blocked the entire river road. Laborers with worn-out shoes wedged stones beneath the wheels; drivers knelt in the mud and cursed. An ox slipped into a ditch, and soldiers hauled it bodily back onto the road by its halter. The men in the rear camps saw only that the column ahead had stopped and assumed the Jin army had arrived. By dusk the rumor had taken three forms: Xie Xuan had hidden ten thousand crossbows on the southern bank; Jin troops had circled behind the Ru River; the emperor was about to cross the Yangtze.

The watermill on the north bank was the first to stop. Its grinding stones had been driven by a narrow channel from the river bend, but soldiers driving piles upstream for the bridge had diverted the current toward the flats, and the wheel turned more slowly by the hour. The miller came early to complain outside the camp. The guards were occupied counting soldiers and told him to return in a few days. He waited until late afternoon, after his family had eaten all the dry cakes they had brought. When Fu Rong, inspecting timber for the bridge, noticed the old man at the gate and learned what had happened, he ordered the workmen to cut another feeder channel without disturbing the bridge’s foundations. The mill reopened, but those waiting for rice in town had already lost a day.

Murong Chui arrested three soldiers in the forward camp for spreading rumors. Rather than treating them as rebels, he sentenced them to carry the wounded for the military doctors through the night. By morning none of the three was eager to talk of miraculous troops across the river.

When Fu Pi climbed the watchtower, the southern bank seemed unnaturally quiet. Xie Xuan had stationed only a few archers near the water. The colors of banners showed faintly behind the woods, and boats came and went. Viewed from afar by the Qin horsemen, the Jin lines looked as thin as paper, ready to fall at a push. But Fu Pi could hear wagons and horses grinding against one another behind and to the side. Those were his own men. The camps stretched for more than ten li and consumed grain and fodder every day.
“If we win one battle at the front, we won’t have to endure all this,” said his attendant.
Fu Pi made no reply. Watching the banners stir gently on the far bank, he felt a vague irritation. Xie Xuan was a clever man. Why would he set out all his soldiers where an enemy could count them?

On the southern bank Xie Xuan’s soldiers were sealing boat hulls with tung oil. People from around Shouchun had brought reeds, bamboo poles, and dried firewood. A young oarsman shared the rice his family had sent with a comrade whose hand was injured, humming a tune from Jiankang as he ate. Xie Xuan entered the boatyard, examined a cracked oar handle, and ordered a craftsman to make another.

Dozens of pale sails hung at the far end of the yard, patched with cloth of differing ages. Xie Xuan ordered the depth each vessel had ridden in the water the previous night recorded on the backs of bamboo tags. Then he picked three boats to carry armored men on a trial crossing of a tributary. The first returned promptly, but the third could not turn in the shallows until two soldiers jumped into the water to push it free. The officer commanding the boats complained about the time wasted. Xie Xuan pointed at the blue fingers of the oarsmen and ordered the boat fitted with a new rudder pin. No one called it a victory when the test ended; wet clothing lay heaped beside the fires.
“General, Qin has five times our numbers. Can one oar more or less change what Heaven has decreed?” an oarsman asked.
“If it breaks in your hands halfway across, it may change what Heaven has decreed for you.”

The oarsman flushed and bent to pick up the cracked shaft. Before leaving, Xie Xuan asked which units had sick men. Told that two rowers had fevers, he ordered replacements. The Beifu Army on the southern bank did not rely on splendid displays. It attended to such small matters every day. The feverish men were withdrawn, and each new oar was tested in the water. Xie Xuan knew that on a river this narrow, once the armies met, there might be no second chance to put a mistake right.

A letter arrived from Xie An in Jiankang. The paper was thin, the handwriting spare. It asked only how long the grain would last, whether boats along the Huai could now pass freely between their routes, and whether the generals in the rear obeyed orders. At the end came a homely question: was Xie Xuan’s eldest son making progress in his studies? Xie Xuan smiled when he read it. He tucked the letter into his robe and ordered scouts to discover the roads used by the Qin baggage train.

Far away in Jiankang, Xie An had earlier inquired into the order in which the Beifu Army received its rations. Grain allotted by the court to Huainan passed through several river checkpoints, whose officers all claimed the right to hold boats for inspection. He had asked the central administration to make the transit documents and seals of the different offices uniform, so a grain boat would no longer have to unload at every city. On hearing of the change, Xie Xuan told his quartermaster to note how many days of delay had been eliminated. The guards outside the tent understood nothing of official seals; they saw only that there was another spoonful of rice in their bowls.

That afternoon an envoy from Jin crossed to the northern bank with a letter from Xie Xuan. The two armies, it said, gained nothing by staring across the water. Would the Qin army draw back a little, allowing the Jin troops to cross and settle matters in battle? The Qin generals broke into argument. Fu Pi thought the enemy was offering itself up for destruction and demanded agreement. Fu Rong first asked how many li they were to retreat, which camps were to move first, and who would use the pontoon bridge. The envoy could not answer.
Fu Jian did not decide at once. He had the envoy escorted to a separate tent and summoned the grain officer, the vanguard’s chief of staff, and Murong Chui.
“Withdraw only the forward ranks,” Fu Pi said. “When the Jin enter the water, let the crossbows fire together. How could we fail to win?”
Murong Chui set an empty cup in front of the sand table and pointed to several cups behind it. “This is the front. It can retreat. But what about these?”
“The rear ranks will make way.”

“The roads are blocked by wagons. If men begin to turn back, those behind cannot see the signal flags; they hear only the horses running. Who will tell them whether the front is luring the enemy or fleeing in defeat?”

Fu Pi was about to retort when the tent flap lifted. Several soldiers escorting grain led in a merchant from the south and made him kneel. The man traded salt along the Huai and said he had seen Jin boats moving through a tributary the day before. Questioned more closely, he could not say whether they were troop vessels or fishing boats. Fu Rong urged that they investigate before letting a single letter disorder the formations. Fu Jian agreed.

Zhu Xu had come south with the Qin army and was lodged in the central camp, though he wore no military uniform. On hearing of the Jin envoy’s challenge, he stood alone before his tent until dusk. The Qin treated him courteously and forbade soldiers to insult him, but he had never consented to advise their army. Fu Jian summoned him and asked about Xie Xuan’s methods of war.

Outside Zhu Xu’s tent stood a few old book chests, their seals still bearing the inventory numbers assigned during his residence in Chang’an. He would not allow his attendants to hide Jin banners and placards among them; nor would he let a Qin staff officer issue him the official papers of a Qin minister. On the road south, refugees from Xiangyang had recognized him. Some knelt before him; others cursed him for remaining alive instead of dying with the city. He merely asked the clerk to enter both their names in the visitors' register. If they sought him after the withdrawal, at least they would know where to find him.
Zhu Xu said, “I am a minister of Jin. If Your Majesty asks about the rivers and passes of the south, I cannot speak.”
“I ask whether, standing on the southern bank, you would invite the enemy to retreat.”
“If I were confident of success, I would.”
“And without that confidence?”
Zhu Xu looked at the emperor. “Perhaps then, too. People brought to the end of their road often have only one test left to make.”

Fu Jian nodded and pressed him no further. He noticed a faded patch on Zhu Xu’s sleeve and asked whether the robe was old. Zhu Xu said he had worn it during the defense of Xiangyang. The cuff had torn, but he had not the heart to throw it away. Fu Jian ordered a new robe sent to him. Zhu Xu declined the gift. The robe was nevertheless left in his tent, untouched throughout the night.

After dark Yao Chang brought a secret report to the imperial tent. Someone, he said, was willing to spread word of a Qin defeat through the rear camps at the moment of withdrawal. The report was vague, naming only a few camp numbers. Fu Jian gave it to an accompanying officer of the Court of Justice for safekeeping and ordered the path of its transmission investigated, without rashly accusing anyone. Yao Chang waited beyond the lamplight and heard the emperor ask only, “Who first told you this?” After a silence, he answered that it had come by word of mouth from former subordinates.
“Can a rumor on men’s lips make me move an army of over a hundred thousand?”
When Yao Chang withdrew, a hard wind was blowing beyond the tent, and the flame inside his lantern shook violently.

Over the next two days the rain continued by fits and starts. Fu Rong sent mounted scouts along the route to the rear. They reported that south of the Ru River the wagon ruts had sunk into deep channels; all the grain wagons could not turn around in a single day. Muster rolls from several camps did not tally. Two cavalry units assigned to the left wing had been sent to guard provisions and had yet to return. Murong Chui brought the old campaign maps before the emperor and checked each point in turn. He refused to offer a reassuring word he could not support.

In the central camp some soldiers had already laid out clothes for the journey home, only to be cursed by their squad leaders and told to put them away. A young man from Hedong heard a companion say that the Jin would be massacred as soon as they withdrew. He grew so frightened that night that he tore loose a tent rope, forcing half the men in the shelter to pitch it again in the rain. The disciplinary officer punished him by making him carry water. At the third bucket, the boy said his elder brother had disappeared along the Huai on the last campaign, and his parents had asked only that he come home alive this time. The officer was silent for a while. Then he told the boy to make sure the remaining knots were tied tight.

At last Fu Jian went in person to the high ground above the northern bank. The southwest wind sent the reeds rustling. The far shore was close enough for him to see someone watering a horse outside the Jin earthworks. Farther off, the treetops stirred on a hillside. Flags appeared and vanished among light and shadow, and there was no telling how many troops might be concealed behind them.
“The crossing is not far from here,” Fu Jian said.
Fu Rong stood beside him. “For a vanguard to cross, it is not far. To take the whole army over—and bring it back—is far.”

Fu Jian turned his gaze to the northern shore. Soldiers who had marched from Luoyang were making camp in the rain. Many had not even seen a Jin soldier’s face, yet were already thousands of li from home. Their ranks were immaculate; only the mud behind the tents betrayed the depth of the wheel tracks. The army’s appearance was no illusion, nor were its supply routes. The danger lay in looking only at the head of the column and forgetting how far the rest of it stretched behind.

The envoy returned to ask what the King of Qin had decided. Fu Jian did not summon the generals to acclaim a victory. He ordered Xie Xuan’s letter, the reports on the road to the rear, and the secret message concerning the intended false rumor laid upon the table, and had every adviser on duty examine them for himself.
Everyone knew that retreat might entice the enemy forward, or throw their own army into chaos. Everyone wanted the emperor to make the wager for them.
Fu Jian looked at the three papers beneath the candle. Just as he was about to speak, the sound of Jin drums came across the water.
